title: Final Essays
description: Ten reflective essays on learning and language: knowing a word, slow reading, the second self, translating a grandmother's letters, rereading, family notebooks, a reporter's vocabulary, surnames, the library at night and the last page of a long book.

lessons.title: What It Means to Know a Word
lessons.summary: An essayist asks when we can say that we know a word, and finds the answer in dictionary prefaces, reading and patience.
lessons.text:
When can we say that we know a word? The question sounds simple, yet the answer keeps moving. The first time I meet a word, I may only recognize its shape. The second time, I guess its meaning from the sentence around it. Weeks later I try it in conversation, and a friend tells me, kindly, that it sounds unnatural there. Did I know the word the first time? Do I know it now?

Dictionary compilers have lived with this question longer than anyone. In the preface to a large dictionary, the short essay in which the compilers explain their methods, one often finds a modest confession: no definition is complete. A compiler can record how a word has been used in thousands of printed sentences, but not every shade of feeling it carries in a single life. I have come to love these prefaces. A preface is where the experts admit what a dictionary cannot do, and that admission seems to me the beginning of real knowledge.

Researchers who study reading describe word knowledge as a slope rather than a door. We do not walk through it once. We climb it progressively, and each meeting with a word moves us a little higher. A word met in a story, then in a letter, then in a news report, gathers meaning as a river gathers water. Each meeting reaffirms what we knew and adds something we did not. This is why immersion works so well. A learner in deep immersion meets the same words again and again, in many settings, and the slope is climbed progressively, almost without effort.

I cannot pinpoint the day I learned most of the words I use. I can pinpoint a few. At twelve, at my grandfather's desk, I looked up the word "melancholy" and felt that someone had finally named a feeling I had carried for years. That recollection is still bright. Yet I do not think I truly knew the word until much later, when I met it in a novel and recognized, with a small shock, my own face in the sentence. The recollection of the first meeting and the experience of the second together made the word mine. The second meeting did not replace the first; it reaffirmed it.

A good dictionary can enlighten us, and so can a good teacher. But a word enlightens us most slowly, a little at each meeting, the way a familiar street looks different in every season. So perhaps the honest answer is that we never finish knowing a word. We only know it better, patiently, year after year, until one day we use it without thinking and it no longer sounds unnatural, but exactly right. That day is worth waiting for patiently.

Questions:
What happens when the writer first tries a new word in conversation?
A friend tells the writer, kindly, that the word sounds unnatural there.
What do compilers often confess in the preface to a large dictionary?
They often confess that no definition is complete.
Why does immersion work so well?
A learner in deep immersion meets the same words again and again, in many settings.
Which word can the writer pinpoint, and when was it learned?
The writer looked up the word "melancholy" at twelve, at the desk of the writer's grandfather.
What is the writer's honest answer to the question in the title?
We never finish knowing a word; we only know it better, patiently, year after year.

lessons.title: Reading as a Slow Conversation
lessons.summary: An essayist describes how medieval monks read a few pages slowly and aloud, and tries their method with a single poem.
lessons.text:
We usually picture reading as a silent, private act: one person, one book, a quiet room. For much of history it was something else. In the monasteries of medieval Europe, reading was slow, spoken and shared, and I have come to think that the monks understood something we have forgotten. A book is less a message than a conversation.

A monastery was led by an abbot, who was usually an ordained priest chosen by the community. The abbot decided what the monks would read and when. In many houses, one monk read aloud during meals while the others ate in silence. Most monks were not ordained; they were ordinary men who had promised to live, work and pray together. Yet every one of them spent part of each day with a book.

What did they read? Above all, the Bible and the writings of the early Church. The letters of the apostles were read again and again, together with commentaries on them. A monk might spend a whole week on one letter of the apostles, reading a few lines each morning, repeating them aloud and carrying them through the day like a stone in his pocket. The study of divinity, as theology was once called, was not a race through many pages but a long return to a few. A student of divinity measured his progress in depth, not in distance.

Reading and prayer were not separate. A monk would kneel in the chapel, then rise and read; later he would kneel again and think about what he had read. Some texts urged the reader to repent, and the monks did not hurry past such lines. To repent, in their understanding, was to turn around and change direction, and a reader who rushed could not turn. Other passages praised righteousness, the steady habit of doing what is right. Righteousness, the monks believed, grew the way their reading grew: a little each day.

There was a sublime side to all this. A copied page might be decorated with gold and blue, so that sublime words had a beautiful home. But the heart of the practice was humble. You read a sentence, you listened, you answered it with your own thoughts, and the next day the sentence answered back.

To a modern reader this may look like folly. Why spend a week on a page when a whole library is waiting? Yet the greater folly may be ours: we read so many pages that we rarely hear any of them speak. Last year I tried the old method with a single poem, reading it each morning for a month. By the end, the poem and I were old friends, and I was not quite the reader who had begun. The conversation had been worth the wait.

Questions:
Who led a monastery?
An abbot led a monastery; he was usually an ordained priest chosen by the community.
How might a monk read a letter of the apostles?
He might spend a whole week on it, reading a few lines each morning and repeating them aloud.
What did it mean to repent, in the monks' understanding?
To repent was to turn around and change direction.
What does the writer call the greater folly?
The greater folly is reading so many pages that we rarely hear any of them speak.
What happened when the writer read one poem each morning for a month?
The poem and the writer became old friends.

lessons.title: The Second Language as a Second Self
lessons.summary: A writer who learned English as a student in London reflects on the calmer, more careful person she became in her second language.
lessons.text:
Many people who speak two languages say that they become a slightly different person in each one. I doubted this until it happened to me.

I grew up speaking Portuguese in a small city in Brazil, and I learned most of my English at twenty, in London, where I spent a year as a student. My landlady, Mrs. Hale, was a retired nurse who kept the telly on from breakfast to bedtime. I learned more from her telly than from my textbooks: the weather, the news and endless games of cricket, which I never understood. Her nephew was a cricketer for a local team, and she explained the rules to me with great patience. "A good cricketer," she said, "can wait all afternoon." I nodded and understood nothing.

On Friday nights we ate takeaway, which is what people in England call takeout. The word itself became a lesson. A takeaway, I discovered, could be a meal, a shop, or, at a meeting, the main idea you carry home.

At the university I practiced in the cafeteria, where students from twenty countries met over cheap coffee. The cafeteria was noisy and friendly, and nobody minded my mistakes. There I noticed something strange. In Portuguese I am a warm, emotional speaker, and I can be grumpy in the morning without apology. In English I was calmer and more careful. I listened more. I made fewer jokes, because jokes are the last thing to arrive in a new language.

Researchers have studied this effect. Some find that bilingual people describe themselves differently depending on the language of the questions. One explanation is simple. Each language is learned in a particular place, among particular people, and it carries their habits with it. My English was learned among patient, polite strangers, and it remains a little patient and polite.

The second self has its weaknesses. When I am tired, my English fails first. Late at night I yawn, lose words and reach for Portuguese, which waits for me like an old coat. Once, at a dinner, I tried to tell a joke in English and got the ending wrong. There was a pause, then a friend gave a loud snort of laughter, and the whole table laughed, not at the joke but at the snort. The laughter was irresistible. I laughed hardest of all, and the evening, which had begun with polite conversation and a yawn or two, became irresistible fun.

Now, after twenty years in the United States, I have stopped asking which self is the real one. Both are. Portuguese gives me the sweetness of childhood, my mother's voice and my grandmother's songs. English gives me a quieter room in which to think. The sweetness and the quiet live together, and I no longer feel that I must choose. Even my grumpy mornings, I have noticed, now happen in two languages.

Questions:
Where did the writer learn most of her English?
She learned most of it at twenty, in London, partly from her landlady's telly.
What did Mrs. Hale say about a good cricketer?
She said that a good cricketer can wait all afternoon.
Why did the writer like to practice in the cafeteria?
The cafeteria was noisy and friendly, and nobody minded her mistakes.
How was the writer different in English?
She was calmer and more careful, she listened more, and she made fewer jokes.
What made the whole table laugh at the dinner?
Her friend's loud snort of laughter made the whole table laugh.

lessons.title: My Grandmother's Letters
lessons.summary: A writer translates the Italian letters his grandmother sent home after she sailed to New York, and learns what translation loses and keeps.
lessons.text:
When my grandmother died, my aunt gave me a box of letters. They were written in Italian, in a careful hand, and most of them were addressed to my grandmother's sister, Rosa, who had stayed behind in their village. After Rosa's death the letters had been sent back across the ocean. I had studied Italian at school, and I decided to translate them, one letter each Sunday.

The first letter was written on the steamer that carried my grandmother to New York in 1921. She was nineteen. She described the steamer as a floating town, crowded and loud, and she complained about the food. "The bread is gray," she wrote, "and I would give anything for one of your pickles." In letter after letter she asked about the jars of pickles in Rosa's cellar, as if they were relatives.

In New York she worked for the proprietor of a small grocery store, and two years later she married him. The proprietor, my grandfather, appears in the letters as a kind, serious man who worked too hard. She wrote about the shop with pride: the barrels, the scales, the big jug of olive oil on the counter, from which customers filled their own bottles. That jug became a character too. When it broke, she mourned it for two letters.

Translation was slow. The hard words were not the long ones but the plain ones. She wrote that she was cooking spinach the way their mother did, with a verb that meant something like "to cook gently until it sighs." No English verb sighs. In the end I wrote that she let the spinach simmer slowly, and I added a note to explain what I had lost. To simmer is close, but it does not sigh. Translators, I learned, are always choosing which loss to accept.

Not every letter was cheerful. In 1930 the shop nearly failed, and she wrote frankly about their misfortune. Yet she wrote more about the plight of the families on her street than about her own. One family had lost everything, and she sent them soup each evening. Their plight worried her more than her own debts. Even in misfortune, she noticed others first.

Her last letters return again and again to the village: the hillside behind the church, the goats on the hillside and the sunflowers that Rosa grew by the door. "Are the sunflowers tall this year?" she asks in one of them. She never went back.

I finished the translation last spring and printed copies for the family. On the cover I put a drawing of a single sunflower, the only picture I could make. Translating her letters did not bring my grandmother back, but it let me hear her voice in two languages, and in both of them she sounded like herself.

Questions:
How did the writer's grandmother travel to New York?
She traveled on a steamer in 1921, when she was nineteen.
What did she miss when she complained about the food?
She missed her sister Rosa's pickles.
Whom did she work for in New York?
She worked for the proprietor of a small grocery store, and later she married him.
Why was the word for cooking spinach hard to translate?
The verb meant "to cook gently until it sighs," and "simmer" does not sigh.
What did she write about during the family's misfortune in 1930?
She wrote more about the plight of the families on her street than about her own.

lessons.title: The Pleasure of Rereading
lessons.summary: A man rereads the adventure novel he loved at eleven and finds that the slow passages he once skipped are now the best ones.
lessons.text:
There is a particular pleasure in rereading a book we loved as children, and a particular risk. The book has not changed, but we have, and we cannot know in advance whether one of us will be disappointed.

When I was eleven, my favorite novel was the story of a young geologist who travels into the rainforest of the Amazon to search for a lost river of gold. I read it four times that year. The geologist was everything I wished to be: a fearless adventurer and a scientist who could read the history of the earth in a broken stone. On the cover, his silhouette stood against a red sunset, a hat on his head and a hammer in his hand. I would stare at that silhouette and imagine myself inside it.

The book captivated me because its plot was unstoppable. Every chapter ended with a danger, and every danger led to the next. Nothing could stop him, and nothing could stop me from reading.

Last winter I found the same edition in a used bookstore and read it again. The first surprise was how short the book was. Chapters I remembered as long journeys were sometimes only four pages. Memory had elongated them, the way the evening sun elongates a shadow until it reaches across a field.

The second surprise was better. As a child I had skipped the slow passages, the ones in which the geologist simply looks around him. Now those passages captivated me most. The author described the rainforest with real care: the layers of leaves, the insects, the birds and a family of small primates watching the camp from the trees. In one scene the geologist sits awake at night and counts the voices he can hear. He realizes that the true treasure of the forest is not gold but life itself, its endless variety. Today we would call it biodiversity, though the author never uses that modern word. I had read that scene four times at eleven without noticing it.

Rereading, I think, shows us two things at once: the book and our former self. The boy who read for the unstoppable plot was not wrong. He read with a hunger I envy. But the man notices the primates in the branches, the biodiversity of a single page and the patience of a writer who stopped the story to look.

When I finished, I looked at the cover again. The silhouette of the adventurer was still there against its red sky. This time I did not want to be him. I was content to be the reader, older and slower, who had finally followed him all the way in.

Questions:
What was the writer's favorite novel about when he was eleven?
It was about a young geologist who travels into the rainforest to search for a lost river of gold.
Why did the book captivate him as a boy?
Its plot was unstoppable: every chapter ended with a danger.
What was the first surprise when he reread the book?
The book was short; memory had elongated the chapters.
What does the geologist realize when he counts the voices at night?
He realizes that the true treasure of the forest is life itself, what we would call biodiversity.
How did the writer feel about the adventurer at the end?
He did not want to be him; he was content to be the reader who had followed him all the way in.

lessons.title: Notebooks and Memory
lessons.summary: A woman and her sister reread the kitchen notebook their mother kept for decades, part cookbook and part family diary.
lessons.text:
Every family has its own way of remembering. Mine kept a notebook in the kitchen drawer.

It began as a cookbook of sorts. My mother bought a plain notebook when she married and started writing down the recipes she wanted to keep. Over the years it became something else: part cookbook, part diary and part record of experimentation. Next to a recipe for lemon cake she would write what went wrong: "too dry, add milk." A week later: "better." The kitchen was her laboratory, and the experimentation never stopped.

Every Sunday we had brunch on the patio, and the brunch was planned in the notebook too. There were lists of guests and notes on who disliked eggs. On one page, in my father's hand, are the instructions for a margarita, which he made for the adults every summer on the patio. The page is stained with lime juice. Beside it my mother wrote: "One margarita each. Your father is not a bartender." It still makes me smile.

The cover tells its own story. When my sister was nine, she painted it with acrylic paints: a yellow sun and three crooked flowers. Acrylic dries quickly and lasts for years, and the flowers are still bright, although the notebook has been opened thousands of times.

Psychologists tell us that memory is not a recording but a reconstruction. Each time we remember, we rebuild the past, and we change it a little. A notebook resists this. It holds the past as it was written, with its mistakes and its handwriting. When I read my mother's notes, I meet not my memory of her but her own voice on an ordinary afternoon.

The notebook also remembers our teamwork. After every brunch there was a cleanup, and the cleanup had rules, written on the back page: my father washed, my mother dried, and my sister and I carried the plates. It was not elegant teamwork, but it was ours.

Some entries are sad. In the year my grandfather was ill, the recipes became simpler and the notes shorter. Yet even there my mother tried to lighten the mood: "Soup again. Nobody complained." A notebook cannot lighten grief, but it can lighten the work of remembering.

My mother is eighty now, and the notebook lives with me. Last month my sister visited, and we sat together on my old sectional sofa with the notebook between us. The sectional is too big for my living room, but it is perfect for two sisters and one book. We turned the pages slowly and read the recipes aloud, and by the end we had decided to bake the lemon cake again. We will write down how it goes.

Questions:
How did the kitchen notebook begin?
It began as a cookbook of sorts, with the recipes the writer's mother wanted to keep.
What did the father make for the adults every summer?
He made a margarita for the adults on the patio.
What is on the cover of the notebook?
There is a yellow sun and three crooked flowers, painted in acrylic by the writer's sister.
What were the rules for the cleanup after brunch?
The father washed, the mother dried, and the two girls carried the plates.
What did the two sisters decide after reading the notebook on the sectional?
They decided to bake the lemon cake again and write down how it goes.

lessons.title: A Reporter's First Vocabulary
lessons.summary: A journalist remembers learning the special language of city government in her first year at a small newspaper.
lessons.text:
When I started as a young reporter at a small newspaper, my editor gave me one piece of advice: learn the language of your beat. A beat is the subject a reporter covers every day, and mine was the city government. I thought I spoke English well. Within a week I discovered that city hall had a language of its own.

The first new words were titles. A staffer, I learned, is someone who works for an elected official, writing speeches and answering calls. The staffers knew more than the officials and said less. A lobbyist is someone paid to persuade officials on behalf of a company or a group. The lobbyists were friendly, well dressed and always available, and my editor warned me to be careful with friendly people.

Then came the words of money. At my first budget meeting, an official spoke for twenty minutes about depreciation. I looked the word up that night. Depreciation, it turned out, is the loss of value that a thing suffers as it ages: a truck, a bridge, a computer. Depreciation explained why the budget always seemed smaller than it looked.

My first real story was about a lake. Fertilizer from nearby farms was washing into it, and the fertilizer contained phosphate. Phosphate feeds the tiny green plants that cover a lake in summer, and when those plants die and decay, they use up the oxygen that fish need. I spent days learning how to explain this in plain language, because a word my readers did not know was a door I had closed in their faces.

In my second month, the city's bus drivers went on strike, and I covered my first picket line. The drivers walked in a slow circle outside the bus station, carrying picket signs. I learned that a reporter must quote both sides fairly. The drivers' union was alleging that the city had broken its promises, and the city was alleging that the union's demands were impossible. My editor read my draft and crossed out every adjective. "Report what they say," he told me. "Let the readers decide."

Language, I discovered, can also be used to neutralize. Officials sometimes chose long, gray phrases to neutralize bad news, so that a plan to close two schools became "an adjustment of facilities." My job was to translate such phrases back into plain English, without anger and without fear.

By the end of the year, my notebook was full of words, and I understood my editor's advice. Learning a beat is like learning a dialect. You listen, you ask, and you write down what you do not know. Then one day you hear an official say "depreciation," and you simply nod. That is when you know you have arrived.

Questions:
What advice did the editor give the young reporter?
He told her to learn the language of her beat.
What is the difference between a staffer and a lobbyist?
A staffer works for an elected official; a lobbyist is paid to persuade officials on behalf of a company or a group.
What does depreciation mean?
Depreciation is the loss of value that a thing suffers as it ages.
How does phosphate harm a lake?
It feeds plants that die and decay and use up the oxygen that fish need.
What were the two sides alleging during the strike?
The union was alleging that the city had broken its promises, and the city was alleging that the union's demands were impossible.

lessons.title: The Trades in Our Names
lessons.summary: An essay on English surnames such as Thatcher and Bowman, which preserve the work of medieval villages.
lessons.text:
Many English surnames are small pieces of history. A person named Baker probably had an ancestor who baked bread, and a person named Cooper had one who made barrels. Our surnames are a dictionary of forgotten work, and reading them is a way of reading the past.

Take the name Thatcher. A thatcher was a craftsman who made roofs from straw or reeds, laying them in thick layers and tying them down so tightly that rain ran off them for decades. In medieval villages most cottages had such roofs, so every region needed a thatcher. Today the trade survives in only a few places, but the name has spread around the world, carried by thousands of families who have never touched straw.

Or take Bowman. A bowman was a soldier who fought with a bow and arrows. In medieval England the bowman was a familiar figure, and the law required ordinary men to practice shooting after church every Sunday. A good bow needed a stout piece of wood and a patient maker. Many bows were made of yew, but some were made of elm, a strong wood that bends without breaking. The arrow was the bowman's projectile, and a skilled archer could send it more than 200 meters. Before guns, an army that could fill the sky with such projectiles was greatly feared.

The elm, too, has its place in names and maps. Many towns in the United States once had an Elm Street, lined with tall elms that met above the road like the roof of a church. Disease killed most of those trees in the last century, but the street names remain, like surnames whose trades have gone.

Building gave us other names. A mason cut and laid stone, and the name Mason is still common. On the great building sites of the Middle Ages, workers would hoist the heavy blocks into place with ropes and huge wooden wheels, turned by men walking inside them. Many stones of an old cathedral were hoisted by human strength, and some of those stout workers passed their trade on as a name.

Modern trades, by contrast, rarely become surnames. Most English families had fixed names by the end of the Middle Ages, and the list has hardly grown since. Thousands of people solder wires every day, joining small pieces of metal with melted metal, yet no family will be named after the people who solder. The age of new surnames ended before the age of electricity began.

I find this comforting. When I meet someone named Thatcher or Bowman, I see behind them a long line of work: wet straw, a bent bow, a stone rising slowly on a rope. A surname is the shortest history book we own, and we carry it everywhere.

Questions:
What did a thatcher do?
A thatcher made roofs from straw or reeds, laying them in thick layers.
What was a bowman?
A bowman was a soldier who fought with a bow and arrows.
Why was elm a good wood for bows?
Elm is a strong wood that bends without breaking.
How did medieval workers hoist heavy stones?
They used ropes and huge wooden wheels, turned by men walking inside them.
Why will no family be named after the people who solder?
Most English families had fixed names by the end of the Middle Ages, before the age of electricity began.

lessons.title: The Library at Night
lessons.summary: A writer remembers two winters of late shifts at a university library and the quiet readers who stayed until closing time.
lessons.text:
For two winters, while I was a graduate student, I worked the late shift at the university library. My job was simple: to answer questions at the front desk, return books to the shelves and lock the doors at midnight. But the real work, I came to feel, was to watch. I am by nature a watcher, and a library at night is a wonderful place for a watcher.

The nightly rhythm rarely changed. At eight the building was full. At ten it was half empty. By eleven only the most determined readers remained, scattered among the long tables like boats on a dark lake. Each had a lamp, and each lamp made a small island of light. Our nightly ritual ended at a quarter to twelve, when I walked through the rooms and quietly announced that the library would close.

I came to know the regulars without learning their names. There was an old man who read only atlases, and a young woman who brought her own cushion. There was a student who fought sleep every night; I would see him stifle a yawn, then another, then give up and rest his head on his book for ten minutes. Late at night everyone was trying to stifle something: a cough, a sigh, a laugh at a funny page. The silence was a shared agreement.

The building had its own life. Some of the oldest shelves had begun to sag under a century of books, and the sagging wood made small sounds when the heating came on. One long shelf of history books sagged in the middle like a tired smile. That winter the library announced a reorganization of the collection, and for weeks we moved thousands of volumes to new shelves. The reorganization was exhausting, but it gave me a chance to hold books that no one had opened in decades.

Only once did anything dramatic happen. One night a pipe burst above the reading room, and the head librarian called me urgently from her home. Water was dripping onto a table of old maps. I carried the maps to a dry room as urgently as I could, and not one of them was damaged.

In spring the library held its yearly book bazaar to sell extra copies, and the old man who loved atlases bought six of them. At the bazaar he spoke to me for the first time. "You are the one who closes the doors," he said. "Thank you for letting us stay until the last minute."

I have worked in many places since, but I still think of those nights. A library at night is not empty. It is full of attention, quiet and shared, and for two winters I had the privilege of watching over it.

Questions:
What was the writer's job at the library?
The writer answered questions, returned books to the shelves and locked the doors at midnight.
What did the writer see a student do every night?
The writer saw him stifle a yawn, then give up and rest his head on his book.
Why did some of the oldest shelves sag?
They had held the weight of a century of books.
What happened when a pipe burst above the reading room?
The head librarian called urgently, and the writer carried the maps to a dry room.
What did the old man say at the book bazaar?
He thanked the writer for letting the readers stay until the last minute.

lessons.title: The Last Page of a Long Book
lessons.summary: Recovering from an operation, a writer finally finishes a thousand-page novel, with a retired teacher in the next bed as company.
lessons.text:
Three years ago I had an operation on my knee, and the doctor told me to expect weeks of rest. I decided to use them well. I packed a long novel that I had started three times and never finished, a book of more than a thousand pages, and I promised myself that I would reach the last page before I walked again.

After the anesthesia my thoughts moved slowly, and I read the same paragraph four times without understanding it. The nurse explained that anesthesia can leave the mind cloudy for a day or two. Then a mild fever arrived. It would fluctuate all week, rising in the evening and falling by morning, and my attention would fluctuate with it.

I shared the room with a retired teacher named Walter, who had a weak heart. He kept a small bottle of nitroglycerin tablets beside his bed. I had known nitroglycerin only as an explosive in old films, and he laughed when I said so. "The same chemical," he said, "in a much smaller dose. It opens the blood vessels." He explained this with the patience of a man who had taught chemistry for forty years.

Walter was a reader too, and he became my companion in the novel. He had read it twice. Every evening he asked where I was, and every evening he was restraining himself, visibly, from telling me what happened next. I was restraining myself as well, from turning to the end. Neither of us wanted to derail the other's pleasure.

Hospitals are not quiet places. Notwithstanding the machines, the voices in the hall and the lights that never fully went off, I read for hours each day. The book was a boon. When the pain began to worsen at night, as pain often does, I opened the novel, and the pain seemed to step back a little. Walter called reading the greatest boon a patient could have. "Better than any pill," he said, "though I would never tell my doctor." Notwithstanding the joke, I think he meant it.

There were small troubles. I developed an intolerance to one of the painkillers, and the doctors had to change it. The intolerance passed in two days, and the pain did not worsen again. Nothing, I had decided, would derail me now.

I reached the last page on the twenty-first day. It was early morning, and the room was gray. I read the final paragraph slowly, then once more, and closed the book. I did not feel triumph. I felt something quieter, like arriving at a house after a long walk and finding the lights on. When Walter woke, I held up the book, and he smiled. "Now you have read it once," he said. "The second time is better."

Questions:
Why did the writer read the same paragraph four times at first?
After the anesthesia, the writer's thoughts moved slowly.
What did Walter keep beside his bed, and why?
He kept nitroglycerin tablets, because he had a weak heart.
Why was Walter restraining himself every evening?
He did not want to tell the writer what happened next in the novel.
What happened when the pain began to worsen at night?
The writer opened the novel, and the pain seemed to step back a little.
How did the writer feel after reading the last page?
The writer felt something quiet, like arriving at a house after a long walk and finding the lights on.
